results.summary: AICD Playground is a mixed-signal test chip developed for the analog IC design course at Graz University of Technology. It integrates an 8-bit digital controller with analog components such as up/down-level shifters, an R2R DAC, and a comparator to form a simple SAR-ADC. The design is programmed via SPI: a mode pin selects between memory initialization and program execution, allowing the CPU to apply voltages through the DAC and read comparator results to implement ADC operation. The design is notable for its educational purpose and includes the TU Graz logo in the layout, but no silicon test results are reported.

Wirecube is a VGA demo that renders a rotating 3D wireframe cube, submitted for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition. It uses an optimized edge function to draw lines by evaluating magnitude thresholds, and stores cube vertices in a ROM to efficiently generate the wireframe. The design outputs VGA signals through a Tiny VGA Pmod and operates at a clock frequency of 50.35 MHz; input pins control background color, cube color, and animation speed. Silicon testing confirmed that the cube rotates and displays effects, though occasionally it stops rotating and turns into a sole rectangle.

This project implements a 3-stage Dickson charge pump that steps up the input voltage to approximately 3.65V, with the output divided by two available on an analog pin. The design uses diodes and capacitors clocked at 2 MHz, but the output is limited by the analog pin voltage constraints (VDDIO/VDDA). Silicon testing by the author shows that the charge pump works but produces much lower voltage than simulation: at 30 MHz, the output peaks at 1.9V instead of the expected 3.6V. The design is a simple power conversion circuit intended for evaluation.

This design generates VGA output to display patterns similar to Ishihara plates used for color blindness testing. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a VGA display, and works out of the box without any configuration. The project is for experimental purposes only and is not an approved medical test. No silicon test results are provided.

Glyph Mode is a standalone VGA demo submitted for the VGA Demoscene competition. It generates a display and allows palette selection via two input pins, choosing between green, red, blue, or pride color schemes. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a VGA monitor, and operates at 25.175 MHz. Silicon tests confirm it works, including palette changes, and it also functions at higher clock speeds.

The Raw_Transistors project provides direct access to raw NMOS and PMOS transistors for performance evaluation. The circuit includes three MOSFETs (two NMOS and one PMOS) with separate gate, source, and drain connections brought out to analog pins. Testing requires a source-measure unit to apply bias voltages and measure currents. Silicon measurements on a TT08 sample confirmed that the transistors work as designed, making it useful for transistor characterization.

This design is a single-tile demo that combines VGA video and audio outputs, created quickly during coffee breaks. It uses a rotozoom effect and plays an attempt at music, with VGA output via a Pmod and audio via an Audio Pmod. Silicon tests confirm that both audio and video work as expected, and testers noted the presence of a Doomguy image, rotozoom, and a bit of E1M1 music, all in one tile. The design operates at 25 MHz and also works at 32 MHz.

This project is a DDR throughput and flop aperture test that grabs data on every clock edge with varying positive pulse widths. It uses positive edge detectors on the clock and its complement to generate two pulses per period, with pulse width adjusted by the number of inverters. The design outputs the captured data and includes a normal flop for comparison. Testing requires an Analog Discovery 3, and the documentation is minimal, with the author stating it works 'badly probably'.

This design is an octal ALU that executes binary operations on two octal numbers encoded in an 8-bit instruction and outputs the result to a 7-segment display. The instruction includes operation code bits and two operands, supporting operations such as addition, subtraction, XOR, AND, and OR. It is used by setting the instruction on the input pins and viewing the result on the 7-segment display; an overflow during addition illuminates the decimal point. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires only the 7-segment display on the TT08 PCB.

This project is a simple 8-bit ALU implemented in Wokwi, featuring a shift register, two registers, and an arithmetic unit capable of addition and subtraction. It uses a bus for data transfer, with control pins to load registers, enable outputs, and select operations; external LEDs display the result in binary. The design is intended for educational purposes, with detailed documentation explaining its operation and testing procedure. Silicon testing confirmed that loading registers and addition work correctly, including a counting example.
